claims.text: In 1974 Robert Spencer Carr publicly claimed alien bodies recovered near Aztec were stored at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson AFB, 'prompting official denials from the Air Force'; in later years 'many accounts, allegedly first-hand, of the Roswell crash contained the Aztec crash story'.

claims.text: The story 'was first published in 1949 by journalist Frank Scully in his Variety magazine columns, and later in his 1950 book Behind the Flying Saucers.'

'The incident gave birth to the Aztec UFO Symposium, which was run by the Aztec, New Mexico, library as a fundraiser from 1997 until 2011.' Revisionist defences were published by Scott Ramsey, Suzanne Ramsey and Frank Thayer as 'The Aztec Incident: Recovery at Hart Canyon' and 'The Aztec UFO Incident'.

claims.text: Per Scully, in March 1948 an unidentified craft 99 feet in diameter containing sixteen humanoid bodies was recovered by the military after a controlled landing in Hart Canyon, 12 miles northeast of Aztec, and 'the military had taken the craft for secret research'.

edges.label: alleged crash site
edges.note: The location is the only fixed and checkable element of the story, and it is the one the town later built a symposium and a plaque around. Silas Newton, lecturing at Denver University on 8 March 1950 as 'Mr. X', claimed to have seen two saucers held by the government, one of which 'crashed near Aztec, New Mexico'; Frank Scully's 'Behind the Flying Saucers' (1950) carried the account, and Newton took Scully touring 'the area where the Aztec saucer ostensibly crashed'. The story ends in court: Newton and Leonard GeBauer were convicted of fraud in 1953 for swindling Herman Flader out of $50,000 with a 'magnetic doodlebug' that cost roughly $3.50 to build, and the 'indestructible' metal was ordinary aluminium.

edges.label: detail donor to later Roswell accounts
edges.note: After the story was revived in the 1970s, its specifics - small bodies, an intact hull, rapid military sanitisation of the site, storage at Wright-Patterson - migrated into allegedly first-hand Roswell testimony. A documented fraud became a supplier of narrative detail to the case the modern disclosure argument rests on, which is a contamination risk this board has to carry explicitly.

edges.label: Air Force denials of Hangar 18 bodies
edges.note: Robert Spencer Carr's 1974 public claim that bodies recovered near Aztec were held at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson AFB drew official Air Force denials. The FBI separately disowned the Guy Hottel memo, the one federal document ever cited as corroboration, in a published 2013 statement.
